transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I came because I just feel flat inside. Even when my children are sitting with me, or the sun is on my garden—things that ought to comfort me—I can’t feel glad or comforted. It’s like that part of me has shut off.
How long have you been feeling this way—unable to feel joy or comfort even in situations that used to bring you pleasure?
About two weeks now. It started after my husband collapsed and the paramedics were working on him in our kitchen.
Since that day, have you been having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about your husband collapsing that feel like you're reliving it?
I’m not sure what you mean by flashbacks. I do think about what happened, of course, but I haven’t noticed feeling like I’m right back there or having nightmares about it.
Since this all began, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—trouble falling asleep, waking up early, or sleeping much more than usual?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid much attention to my sleep, honestly.
Over these past two weeks, have you noticed your energy level changing—do you feel unusually tired or drained most of the day, even without much exertion?
I’m not sure, to be honest. I haven’t really noticed whether my energy is different.
Over these past two weeks, would you say you've been feeling down or low for most of the day, nearly every day, or does your mood tend to lift at times when you're distracted or with your family?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really been paying attention to whether I feel down all day or if it changes when I’m with family.
Since your husband's collapse, have you been having thoughts that you are worthless, or blaming yourself for what happened, even if it wasn't your fault?
I don’t know… I haven’t really thought about it in that way.
Have you ever had a period like this before—weeks of feeling flat, joyless, or down—at any other point in your life, even years ago?
I don’t know about before. But now, even when my children are sitting with me or the sun is on my garden, I just feel flat inside. Like the part of me that could feel glad or comforted has shut off.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over the past two weeks—eating much more or much less than usual?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed whether I’m eating more or less, or any change in my weight.
Over these past two weeks, has this flat feeling made it hard for you to manage your usual daily activities—like cooking, caring for your children, or household tasks?

Yes. I’ve stopped going to the senior center, and I can’t seem to manage meals, errands, or even my calendar without my daughter stepping in. Mostly I just stay in the house. I avoid the kitchen unless someone is there with me.

When you avoid the kitchen unless someone is with you, is that because being there reminds you of your husband collapsing and makes you feel distressed, or is it more that you just don't have the energy or interest to be in there at all?
I’m not sure, really. I just find myself staying out of there unless someone else is around.
Aside from situations that remind you of your husband's collapse, do you also feel this same flatness and inability to enjoy things in other parts of your day that have nothing to do with that event?
Yes. Even when my children are sitting with me, or the sun is out on my garden, I just feel flat inside. It’s like the part of me that could feel glad or comforted has shut off.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or feeling like life isn't worth living since your husband's collapse?
I’m not sure what you mean. I’ve been feeling very flat, but I haven’t really thought about that in those terms.
Have you noticed yourself moving, speaking, or thinking more slowly than usual, or conversely feeling restless and unable to sit still?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself being especially restless, and I can’t say whether I’m moving or talking slower.
Would you say your ability to look after yourself—like bathing, dressing, or basic self-care—has also been affected, or is it mainly household tasks and errands that have become difficult?

It’s more than just errands. I’ve stopped going to the senior center, and I mostly stay in the house. I can’t manage meals or keep track of my calendar without my daughter stepping in. I avoid the kitchen unless someone is with me.
Have you found it hard to do things like bathing, dressing, or brushing your teeth yourself, or are you still able to manage those basic personal care tasks on your own?

I can still manage things like bathing and getting dressed. It’s the other things that have become too much—meals, errands, remembering what I’m supposed to do. My daughter has to step in, and I mostly just stay at home.

Even with your daughter's help, would you say you're still able to push through and complete some of your daily tasks with great difficulty, or does it feel like it's almost impossible for you to carry out any of these activities at all right now?

It feels almost impossible on my own. I don’t go to the senior center anymore, and I can’t keep up with meals, errands, or my calendar unless my daughter steps in. Mostly I just stay in the house, and I won’t go in the kitchen unless somebody is with me.

patient.answer: It feels almost impossible on my own. I don’t go to the senior center anymore, and I can’t keep up with meals, errands, or my calendar unless my daughter steps in. Mostly I just stay in the house, and I won’t go in the kitchen unless somebody is with me.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a two-week history of pervasive anhedonia and emotional numbing (unable to feel joy or comfort even with family or pleasant stimuli), occurring both in trauma-related contexts and unrelated contexts, following a severe acute stressor (witnessing husband's medical collapse). This pervasive, generalized anhedonia rather than trauma-specific avoidance argues against PTSD/Acute Stress Disorder, and the presence of marked functional impairment (unable to manage meals, errands, calendar, stopped attending senior center, requires daughter's assistance) without psychotic features supports a severe single depressive episode. Criteria for re-experiencing symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares) were explicitly denied, making PTSD unlikely. While several vegetative symptoms (sleep, appetite, energy, psychomotor changes) were not clearly endorsed due to patient's uncertainty, the core symptom of anhedonia is severe and pervasive, and functional impairment is severe (near inability to carry out daily activities independently), consistent with severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms (F32.2).
